In a food chain, what do producers provide for the rest of the living things?
Food energy made from sunlight
Only shade and cooler air
Nothing useful for animals
Only rocks and minerals
Producers such as plants capture sunlight and make food. That food energy then moves to animals that eat plants and to animals that eat other animals.
Energy moves from producers to consumers along a food chain.
Why are many bats active at night instead of during the day?
There is less competition and danger from daytime hunters
Their ears only work in bright sunlight
They must drink salt water every hour
They can live only underwater
Many bats hunt at night when fewer daytime predators are active and when their night-hunting senses work well.
Nocturnal animals are active mainly at night.
Bats often use hearing and echolocation to find food in the dark.
What is the main job of the digestive system?
Break food down so the body can use nutrients
Carry oxygen into every bone
Pump air out of the lungs only
Keep the body cold in every season
The digestive system breaks food into smaller pieces and nutrients the body can absorb and use for energy and growth.
Digestion breaks food into usable nutrients.
Organs such as the stomach and intestines help digest food.
What does the heart do?
It pumps blood through the body
It makes all the light we see
It covers the body like skin
It stores unused food forever
The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood so oxygen and nutrients can reach body cells.
The heart is part of the circulatory system.
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
Water helps body systems work and stay balanced
Water replaces the need for sleep
Water turns bones into metal
Water stops the heart from beating
Water helps transport materials, control temperature, and keep cells and organs working well.
The body is made of a large amount of water.
Drinking water supports healthy body function.
Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide
Digest all the food you eat
Control eyesight in bright light
Make new bones grow longer
When you breathe, the lungs take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide as a waste gas.
The lungs are the main organs of breathing.
Oxygen from air moves into the blood in the lungs.
Where does most of the energy your body uses come from?
Food you eat
Only the color of your clothes
Sounds you hear
Shadows on the wall
Food provides chemical energy. Digestion and body processes turn that energy into fuel for movement, growth, and warmth.
Food is the body's main energy source.
Nutrients from food help cells do work.
How does oxygen get from the lungs to the rest of the body?
Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to body cells
Blood carries light from the eyes to the toes
Blood turns oxygen into solid rock
Oxygen travels only through the hair
Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs. Circulating blood then delivers that oxygen to cells throughout the body.
The circulatory system moves blood around the body.
Red blood cells help carry oxygen.
Why do working muscles need a steady supply of oxygen?
Oxygen helps muscles release energy from nutrients
Oxygen paints the muscles a new color
Oxygen replaces bones during exercise
Oxygen stops muscles from ever resting
Active muscles need more energy. Oxygen helps cells release energy from food so muscles can keep working.
Muscle cells use oxygen to make energy.
Breathing and blood flow increase during hard activity.
What is an important job of the kidneys?
Pump oxygen straight into the ears
Store sunlight under the skin
Heat the body by burning bones
Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water, which leave the body as urine.
Kidneys are part of the excretory system.
Healthy kidneys help keep blood chemistry balanced.
What does the nervous system mainly do?
Send messages between the brain, senses, and body parts
Digest food in the stomach only
Make light for the eyes
Carry blood instead of the heart
Nerves and the brain carry signals that help you sense the world, think, and control movement.
The nervous system includes the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
Nerve signals travel quickly through the body.
It gently prepares muscles for stronger activity
It removes the need for oxygen
It turns muscles into bone
It stops the heart from pumping
A warm-up increases blood flow and loosens muscles so they are ready for harder movement and less likely to strain.
Warm muscles work more safely during exercise.
Light activity before a workout prepares the body.
What is one important job of the skin?
Protect the body and help sense touch
Make light for night vision
Pump blood to the lungs
Digest food in the mouth
Skin is a protective covering. It also helps with touch sensing and helps control body temperature.
Skin is the body's outer protective layer.
Nerve endings in the skin detect touch, heat, and pain.
What does your pulse mainly tell you about?
How long your hair is growing
How much light your eyes store
How thick your skin feels
A pulse is the throb you feel when blood is pushed by each heartbeat. Counting it shows heart rate.
Pulse rate rises during exercise and strong feelings.
Heartbeats push waves of blood through arteries.
What is the main job of blood vessels?
Carry blood to and from body parts
Create images in the eyes
Make sounds for hearing
Store unused air in bones
Arteries, veins, and capillaries form pathways that move blood around the body.
Blood vessels are tubes that transport blood.
The heart and vessels work together as a system.
Why do body cells need oxygen?
To help release energy from food nutrients
To turn hearing into sight
To replace water with sand
To stop all chemical reactions
Cells use oxygen in processes that release energy from nutrients so the body can work and stay alive.
Cellular respiration uses oxygen to help make usable energy.
Without enough oxygen, cells cannot work well.
A testable idea about what might happen
The final score of a sports game
A list of tools with no purpose
A drawing that cannot be checked
A hypothesis is an educated guess you can test with an experiment and evidence.
Scientists write hypotheses before testing ideas.
Results can support or not support a hypothesis.
Why do scientists change only one variable at a time in a fair test?
So they can tell what caused the result
So every measurement becomes identical forever
So they never need to record data
So the experiment finishes without tools
If too many things change at once, you cannot know which change caused the outcome.
A fair test keeps most conditions the same.
The independent variable is the one you purposely change.
Why should you write down what happens during an experiment?
A clear log helps you remember and share results
Notes make the equipment heavier
Writing replaces the need for safety
Logs turn water into ice instantly
Recording observations and measurements lets you check your work and compare results later.
Scientists keep careful records of procedures and data.
Good notes make experiments easier to repeat.
To check whether the results are reliable
To invent a new planet each time
To avoid measuring anything
To erase all earlier evidence
Repeating a test helps show whether results happen again and are not just a lucky accident.
Reliable results can be repeated under similar conditions.
Repeating trials reduces the chance of a one-time mistake.
Why do scientists use standard units when they measure?
So others can understand and compare the measurements
So every object becomes the same size
So no tools are ever needed
So experiments never need safety rules
Units such as centimeters, grams, and degrees Celsius let people share clear, comparable data.
Standard units make measurements meaningful to others.
Using the right unit matches the kind of measurement.
What is a control in many science experiments?
A comparison setup that does not get the tested change
A rule that bans all measuring tools
A guess that can never be checked
A chart with no labels at all
A control group or control setup shows what happens without the tested change, so you can compare results fairly.
Controls help scientists see the effect of one change.
Comparing treatment and control makes conclusions stronger.
What is the most important reason to follow safety rules in a lab?
To protect people and prevent accidents
To make experiments finish faster only
To avoid writing any observations
To keep results secret from everyone
Safety rules reduce harm from spills, heat, sharp tools, and other lab risks.
Wear safety gear when a procedure calls for it.
Ask an adult before using unfamiliar lab materials.
Which trait do mammals usually share?
They have hair or fur and feed milk to their young
They breathe only with gills in water
They are covered only in dry scales and never grow hair
They make food from sunlight like green plants
Mammals are warm-blooded animals with hair or fur. Mothers produce milk for their babies.
Dogs, cats, whales, and humans are mammals.
Milk feeding is a key mammal trait.
What kind of eater is a cow?
A herbivore that mainly eats plants
A carnivore that eats only meat
An animal that never needs food
A producer that makes sunlight
Cows eat grass and other plants, so they are herbivores.
Herbivores eat plants.
Cows have teeth suited for chewing plant material.
What helps fish live successfully in water?
They use gills to take oxygen from water
They grow lungs that only work in deserts
They drink only boiling water
They make nests from dry leaves only
Fish take dissolved oxygen from water through gills and have bodies shaped for swimming.
Gills let fish breathe underwater.
Fins help fish move and keep balance.
